$comment: Single source of truth for design §6.1/§6.2 module boundaries. Consumed by packages/config/eslint/node.mjs (static enforcement) and by the boundary test in apps/api (table ownership). Every §7.2 table appears in exactly one module's `owns` list, or in `shared`. A module directory missing from `modules[]` is invisible to moduleOfPath, so its edges are allowed by default: `m25-workflow-egress` is in that state (see ADR-BE-18, deferred work). Registering a module is a deliberate edit, never a silent default.

shared.$comment: Tables with more than one legitimate writer. Only the named repository may write them; the boundary test still checks that no module defines its own DDL-owning repository for these.

runtime.$comment: Directories under apps/api/src that are platform machinery rather than a product domain, yet still name tables. They were a hard-coded map inside the boundary test; declaring them here means a new directory cannot avoid the rule by being new, and the test stops special-casing TypeScript. `audit` and `secrets` are absent because they are now `modules/m17-audit` and `modules/m15-secrets`, where their contracts already were.
NFR-4.16: the image-trust guard runs inside common/docker, so the cached allow-list reader names that one table. M02 still owns the writes and the audit row.
The job surface owns the queue tables in practice (M05 declares them because a deployment is what fills them); `instance` and `idp_user` are read for the labels the job screen shows.

modules.name: Catalog
modules.$comment: FR-2.14: `verified_by` records the reviewer's name, so the catalog resolves a subject id against the identity mirror the way M10 and M18 do. M08 still owns `idp_user` and every write to it.

modules.name: Source Resolver
modules.$comment: NFR-4.16: the allow-list is source policy, so the module that evaluates compose/Dockerfile evidence also owns its revision rows. The pull/build guard in common/docker reads the same state through this module's reader rather than holding a copy.

modules.name: Executor
modules.$comment: M05 builds the instance read model, so it reads the evidence the other modules own rather than a copy of it: `backup`/`backup_schedule` (M16) are read because the fleet list and the detail header state the backup posture, and the document in `instance.payload` is only a fallback for rows no schedule or backup set has been recorded against yet. M16 still owns the writes.

modules.name: Integration
modules.$comment: M03 is the edge that makes a client secret real: the product reads it from `instance_env_value`, which M03 owns, so `ensureIdentitySecret` writes through M03's contract instead of this module's SQL.

modules.name: Identity Sync
modules.$comment: M15 is the product admin token for the FR-2.4 role push: the secret store is the only place a product credential may live, and opening it is audited.

modules.name: Access Control
modules.$comment: `workflow`/`workflow_run` are reads, not an edge: FR-5.9 decides scope by the products a definition writes to, so the PDP must resolve a workflow (or one of its runs) to instances without depending on M13.

modules.name: Workflow
modules.$comment: FR-5.9 needs two facts this module does not own: the live role bindings (M09) and the break-glass elevations an R1 write leans on (M18). Both are read through their contracts. FR-5.8 adds one more edge: the owner failure alert is delivered by M20, through its interface (ADR-BE-30).

modules.name: Capacity
modules.$comment: FR-4.5: `instance_usage_sample` is the measured half of the board. The owner is M05 because it is the module that reads the containers and writes the row; M19 only reads the newest sample per instance.

modules.name: Notification
modules.$comment: FR-4.5 adds the consumption samples (the threshold rule) and `catalog_entry` (FR-4.11: the domain owner the break-glass notice is addressed to). Both are reads; M20 writes only its own two tables.

modules.name: Observability Fabric
modules.$comment: FR-2.6/AC-45: the profile writer owns `observability_profile`; the report and exposition read the instance read model and the newest consumption sample. `instance` was absent while the module was contract-only, which is how the gap survived review.
